cards.q: When the two sets of fans began shouting at each other, the captain walked over, joked with both sides and ___.
o: added more fuel to the fire
cards.why: Joking with both sides eased the tension. Adding fuel to the fire and throwing down the gauntlet would have made it worse, and faint praise would have stung both sides.

idioms.meaning: A sharp remark made while leaving, so that no reply is possible
idioms.origin: Parthian horse archers (in ancient Persia) would pretend to retreat, then turn in the saddle and shoot at their pursuers. The more common 'parting shot' probably grew out of it.
idioms.caption: Riding away, still firing.

cards.q: Walking out of the meeting, the director fired a Parthian shot: 'Next time, read the report first.' What was it?
o: A cutting remark made on the way out
A formal warning given in writing
A threat to resign from the company
A joke meant to ease the tension
cards.why: A Parthian shot is a sting delivered while leaving, so no one can answer back.

cards.q: As she stepped off the debate stage, she turned and delivered ___: 'At least my facts were real.'
cards.why: A barbed line fired while walking away is a Parthian shot.

words.meaning: Eager to fight or argue; aggressively defiant
words.note: Latin trux, trucis = fierce, savage.

cards.q: Asked about the delay, the minister turned ___, jabbing a finger at reporters and refusing every follow-up.
cards.why: Jabbing a finger and refusing questions is aggressive defiance. Tractable means easy to manage (the opposite), tremulous means trembling and translucent means letting light through.

o: The truculent bouncer squared up to anyone who questioned his rules.
Her truculent voice was so soft the back rows strained to hear it.
The truculent stream trickled gently past the sleepy village.
He was too truculent to argue, so he agreed with everyone in the room.
cards.why: Truculent means ready for a fight. The other sentences use it to mean soft, gentle and meek, which is close to the opposite.

words.meaning: A person who flatters powerful people to win favour
words.note: Greek sykophantes, originally an informer in ancient Athens. The flattery sense developed later.

cards.q: He laughs loudest at the boss's jokes, praises every half-baked idea and never once disagrees in a meeting. What is he?
cards.why: Flattering the powerful to win favour is what a sycophant does. A charlatan fakes expertise, a dilettante dabbles without depth and a misanthrope dislikes people in general.

cards.q: Surrounded by ___ who called every plan brilliant, the CEO never heard the warnings until the company collapsed.
cards.why: People who praise every plan are flatterers, which is why he never heard the warnings. Iconoclasts, dissenters and mavericks would all have challenged him.

words.meaning: Stubbornly refusing to obey authority or follow instructions
words.note: Latin recalcitrare = to kick back, like a mule (calx = heel).

cards.q: Even after three warnings, the ___ tenant refused to move out or pay the arrears.
cards.why: Refusing despite repeated warnings is stubborn defiance: recalcitrant. Recriminatory means making counter-accusations, recumbent means lying down and reticent means reserved in speech.

o: The recalcitrant pupil ignored every rule the new teacher set.
The recalcitrant volunteer cheerfully agreed to every task on the list.
A recalcitrant breeze drifted gently through the open window.
Her recalcitrant memory recalled every date without any effort.
cards.why: Recalcitrant means stubbornly disobedient. The wrong sentences use it to mean willing, gentle and reliable.

words.meaning: Quick to notice and understand things that others miss
words.note: Latin perspicax = sharp-sighted (perspicere = to see through). Don't confuse with perspicuous, which means clearly expressed.

cards.q: A detective glances at a visitor's sunburnt neck and worn boots and correctly guesses he has just returned from a trek. Which word best describes her?
cards.why: Seeing what others overlook is perspicacious. Impressionable means easily influenced, superstitious means believing in omens and pertinacious means stubbornly persistent.

o: A perspicacious editor caught a flaw three reviewers missed.
The perspicacious fog made it impossible to see the end of the road.
He was so perspicacious that he believed every rumour he heard.
The essay was perspicacious: long, rambling and hard to follow.
cards.why: Perspicacious means sharply perceptive. The wrong sentences use it to mean foggy, gullible and muddled.

words.meaning: Harmful to something, or unfriendly and hostile
words.note: Latin inimicus = enemy (in- not + amicus friend). Same root as enemy.

cards.q: Constant notifications are ___ to deep work; every ping resets your concentration.
cards.why: Notifications harm concentration, so inimical. Inimitable means impossible to copy, intrinsic means built-in and incidental means minor or accompanying.

o: A culture of fear is inimical to honest feedback in any team.
Her inimical smile made every guest feel instantly welcome.
The two friends were inimical, sharing everything since school.
The recipe is inimical, so nobody has ever managed to copy it.
cards.why: Inimical means harmful or hostile. The wrong sentences use it to mean warm, close and inimitable (impossible to copy).

idioms.meaning: A 'choice' where you take what is offered or get nothing
idioms.origin: Thomas Hobson, a 17th-century Cambridge stable owner, made customers take the horse nearest the door or none at all.
idioms.caption: That horse, or no horse.

cards.q: With only one bus a day out of the village, commuters faced a Hobson's choice. What does that mean?
o: No real choice: take it or nothing
A choice between two equally bad options
A choice made in a hurry, without thought
A choice that seems easy but is a trap
cards.why: One bus, take it or stay put: that is Hobson's choice. It isn't a choice between two bad options (that would be a dilemma), because there is only one option.

cards.q: The canteen serves one dish a day, so lunch is always ___: eat the dal or go hungry.
cards.why: Take the one thing offered or nothing. A curate's egg is something partly good and partly bad, which is about quality, not choice.

idioms.meaning: Take a step that commits you and cannot be undone
idioms.origin: In 49 BC Julius Caesar led his army across the Rubicon river into Italy, breaking Roman law and making civil war certain.
idioms.caption: Once across, there is no going back.

cards.q: When she resigned and posted her farewell on the company forum, she knew she had crossed the Rubicon. What does that mean?
o: She had made a move she could not take back
She had reached the high point of her career
She had openly broken a company rule
She had travelled far from where she began
cards.why: A public resignation can't be undone. The idiom is about an irreversible commitment, not success or rule-breaking as such.

cards.q: Once the founders signed the merger and dissolved the old company, they had ___; there was no way back.
cards.why: 'No way back' is the key: crossing the Rubicon is an irreversible step. Grasping the nettle means facing a difficulty boldly and cutting the Gordian knot means solving a tangle in one stroke; neither stresses irreversibility.

words.meaning: Stubbornly refusing to change one's mind, even when appealed to
words.note: Latin obdurare = to harden (durus = hard, as in durable).

cards.q: Despite tearful appeals from the families, the ___ official would not reopen the case.
cards.why: Unmoved by tearful appeals: obdurate. Obsequious means fawning, obliging means willing to help, and obtuse means slow to understand, which is not the same as refusing.

o: The obdurate referee stood by his call despite the replay.
The obdurate child changed his mind the moment anyone asked him.
The obdurate witness forgot his own name halfway through the trial.
An obdurate guest, he happily ate whatever the host served him.
cards.why: Obdurate means stubbornly unmoved. The wrong sentences use it to mean easily persuaded, forgetful and accommodating.

words.meaning: Physical or mental weariness; a lack of energy
words.note: Latin lassus = weary.

cards.q: After weeks of night shifts, a deep ___ settled over her; even reading a page felt like hard work.
cards.why: Finding even a page hard work is weariness: lassitude. Latitude means freedom of action (or a map line), longitude is a map line and plenitude means abundance.

cards.q: A student who once loved debate now drags himself to class, yawns through every session and can't summon the energy to start his homework. What is he suffering from?
cards.why: No energy and constant weariness is lassitude. Apprehension is anxiety, indignation is anger at unfairness and ambivalence is having mixed feelings.

words.meaning: Strict honesty and moral uprightness
words.note: Latin probitas, from probus = good, honest. Shares a root with prove.

cards.q: A judge's ___ must be beyond question; even a hint of a bribe can end a career.
cards.why: A judge must be honest beyond question: probity. Propensity and proclivity both mean a tendency, and profundity means depth of thought.

o: His probity made him return the extra change he was given.
Her probity showed in how quickly she could solve the puzzle.
The probity of the soil made the crops grow unusually fast.
He was known for his probity, lying whenever it suited him.
cards.why: Probity is honesty. The wrong sentences use it for quick thinking, fertility and, absurdly, dishonesty.

words.meaning: Willing to act dishonestly for money; open to bribery
words.note: Latin venalis = for sale. Don't confuse with venial, a minor, forgivable fault.

cards.q: The ___ clerk would lose your file unless you slipped him a few hundred rupees.
cards.why: Demanding money to do his job means he is open to bribery: venal. Venial means minor and forgivable, venous relates to veins and vernal relates to spring.

o: A venal inspector passed the building in return for cash.
Forgetting her birthday was a venal slip, easily forgiven by all.
The venal garden burst into full blossom early in March.
The doctor carefully checked the venal blood flow in his arm.
cards.why: Venal means bribable. The others confuse it with venial (forgivable), vernal (of spring) and venous (of veins).

words.meaning: Deeply embarrassing and shameful, especially in public
words.note: Latin ignominia = loss of one's good name (in- not + nomen name).

o: The team's ignominious exit drew jeers from its own fans.
Her ignominious design for the bridge won the national award.
He gave an ignominious speech that everyone praised for hours.
His ignominious trust in strangers made him easy to cheat.
cards.why: Ignominious means publicly shameful. The wrong sentences use it to mean brilliant, admirable and naive (ingenuous).

cards.q: A minister who campaigned on honesty is caught on camera taking cash and resigns amid public ridicule. How would you describe his fall?
cards.why: A public, shameful fall is ignominious. Innocuous means harmless, inadvertent means accidental and idiosyncratic means peculiar to one person.

idioms.meaning: A sudden, complete change of opinion or belief
idioms.origin: From the Bible: Saul, a persecutor of Christians, was struck by a blinding light on the road to Damascus and became the apostle Paul.
idioms.caption: One moment on the road, and everything turns.

cards.q: The senator, a lifelong opponent of solar subsidies, had a Damascene conversion after visiting a drought-hit district. What happened?
o: He suddenly and completely changed his view
He pretended to change his view for votes
He slowly softened his view over many years
He was forced by his party to change his view
cards.why: Damascene stresses a change that is both sudden and complete. Pretending, or softening slowly, misses one or both parts.

cards.q: The former junk-food blogger now runs marathons and preaches clean eating; friends call it ___.
o: the thin end of the wedge
cards.why: A total turnaround in belief and behaviour. A Faustian bargain trades one's values for gain, which is nearly the opposite of a sincere change of heart.

idioms.meaning: Pretending you never wanted something after failing to get it
idioms.origin: Aesop's fable: a fox that can't reach some grapes walks off saying they were probably sour anyway.
idioms.caption: Couldn't reach them, so they must be sour.

cards.q: After failing to make the cricket team, Rohan told everyone the coach plays favourites and the team is useless anyway. His friends said it was sour grapes. Meaning?
o: He was belittling what he couldn't get
He was rightly exposing unfair selection
He was jealous of the players who did well
He was hiding how much the loss hurt him
cards.why: Sour grapes is running something down because you failed to get it. Jealousy and hurt pride are related feelings, but the idiom is specifically about disparaging the prize.

cards.q: When she didn't get the promotion, she announced that the new role was all paperwork and no fun. It sounded like ___.
cards.why: Belittling the role she missed out on is sour grapes. Crocodile tears are fake sorrow, and damning with faint praise is criticising through weak compliments.

words.meaning: Difficult to understand; obscure
words.note: Latin abstrusus = hidden, thrust away.

cards.q: The lecture on quantum field theory was so ___ that even the PhD students struggled to follow it.
cards.why: Hard to follow means abstruse. Obtuse describes a person who is slow to understand, abstemious means restrained in eating and drinking, and astute means shrewd.

o: Her abstruse notes on tax law baffled even the senior lawyers.
The abstruse instructions were so simple a child could follow them.
He was too abstruse to notice the hint, so she spelled it out.
The abstruse diner ate only one small meal a day.
cards.why: Abstruse means hard to understand. The wrong sentences use it to mean simple, slow-witted (obtuse) and self-denying (abstemious).

words.meaning: Excessively talkative, especially about trivial things
words.note: Latin garrire = to chatter.

cards.q: The ___ taxi driver narrated his entire family history before we had even left the airport.
cards.why: Talking nonstop about trivia is garrulous. Gregarious means sociable and fond of company, which doesn't require endless talk; querulous means complaining and gracious means courteous.

o: A garrulous neighbour turns a quick hello into a long chat.
The garrulous monk had not spoken a single word in eleven years.
Her garrulous handwriting was neat, small and easy to read.
He felt garrulous after the long climb and sat down to rest.
cards.why: Garrulous means overly talkative. The wrong sentences use it for silence, neatness and tiredness.

words.meaning: Mentally or physically inactive; sluggish
words.note: Latin torpere = to be numb. The noun is torpor.

cards.q: After the heavy wedding lunch, the guests sat ___ in the afternoon heat, barely able to keep their eyes open.
cards.why: Barely awake after a heavy meal is sluggish inactivity: torpid. Torrid means scorching or passionate, turgid means swollen or pompous and tepid means lukewarm.

cards.q: The economy remained ___ for two years, with factories idle and almost no new hiring.
cards.why: Idle factories and no hiring describe sluggish inactivity. Buoyant and robust mean thriving, and volatile means swinging unpredictably.

words.meaning: Complaining in a whining, petulant way
words.note: Latin queri = to complain. Same root as quarrel.

cards.q: On every trip, Uncle Mohan grumbles that the train is late, the tea is cold and the seats are hard, always in the same whining tone. Which word describes him?
cards.why: Constant whining complaint is querulous. Quizzical means mildly puzzled or amused, credulous means too ready to believe and quixotic means idealistic and impractical.

o: The querulous patient grumbled about every meal she was served.
His querulous question showed he had read the chapter with care.
The querulous puppy wagged happily at every stranger it met.
A querulous breeze carried the scent of jasmine through the room.
cards.why: Querulous means whiny and complaining. The wrong sentences use it to mean careful, cheerful and pleasant.

words.meaning: Make an unpleasant feeling less intense; satisfy (hunger or thirst)
words.note: Latin ad + suavis = sweet: literally, to sweeten.

cards.q: The CEO's personal apology did little to ___ the anger of customers who had lost their savings.
cards.why: To lessen anger is to assuage it. You assure a person, not their anger; aggravate means make worse (which 'did little to' rules out), and assess means evaluate.

o: A cup of hot chai helped assuage her worry before the result.
He assuaged the stubborn stain with soap, but it would not budge.
The teacher assuaged the paper and gave it a fair grade.
They assuaged the ladder against the wall and climbed up.
cards.why: Assuage means to ease a feeling. The wrong sentences use it to mean scrub, assess and lean.

idioms.meaning: Caught between two dangers, where avoiding one means facing the other
idioms.origin: In Homer's Odyssey, Odysseus had to sail a narrow strait between Scylla, a six-headed monster, and Charybdis, a deadly whirlpool.
idioms.caption: Steer away from one, straight into the other.

cards.q: Raise interest rates and growth stalls; hold them and inflation runs wild. The central bank is between Scylla and Charybdis. Meaning?
o: Any move it makes leads to a danger
It cannot decide what it wants to do
It is trapped by its own past mistakes
Two rival groups are pulling it apart
cards.why: Both options carry real danger. It isn't indecision or past mistakes; every route leads into some harm.

cards.q: The coach could drop his star player and lose the match, or play him injured and risk his career. He was ___.
o: living under the sword of Damocles
cards.why: Two choices, each with serious harm. The sword of Damocles is one looming threat hanging over you, not a forced choice between two.

idioms.meaning: Something that distracts attention from the real issue
idioms.origin: Strong-smelling smoked (red) herring was said to be dragged across a trail to throw hounds off the scent; William Cobbett popularised the image in 1807.
idioms.caption: The hounds chase the smell, not the fox.

cards.q: In the mystery novel, the missing butler turns out to be a red herring. What does that tell you?
o: He's a false clue that misleads the reader
He's the real culprit hiding in plain sight
He's a minor character with no role at all
He's the victim of the crime in the story
cards.why: A red herring pulls attention away from the truth. It isn't simply an unimportant character; it actively misleads.

cards.q: Instead of explaining the budget overrun, the minister kept talking about the opposition's record, a classic ___.
cards.why: Changing the subject to distract from the real issue is a red herring. A Trojan horse is a hidden threat disguised as a gift.

words.meaning: Eager to fight; aggressively hostile, especially between nations
words.note: Latin bellum = war, also seen in belligerent and antebellum.

cards.q: The general's ___ speech, full of threats against the neighbouring country, alarmed diplomats everywhere.
cards.why: Threats against a neighbour are warlike: bellicose. Benevolent means kind, bucolic means rural and peaceful, and verbose means wordy; a speech can be wordy without being threatening.

o: The bellicose tweets from both leaders raised fears of open war.
The bellicose lullaby soon sent the baby gently off to sleep.
Her bellicose cake was so rich that nobody could finish a slice.
The bellicose shepherd led his flock to graze on the quiet hill.
cards.why: Bellicose means eager for war or a fight. The wrong sentences use it to mean soothing, rich and peaceful.

words.meaning: A bitter, forceful verbal attack
words.note: Greek diatribe = a way of passing time, then a lecture. The hostile sense came later.

cards.q: What began as a polite complaint turned into a ten-minute ___ against the airline, its staff and its food.
cards.why: A long, bitter attack 'against' something is a diatribe. A dialogue involves two sides, a digression wanders off topic and a diagnosis identifies a problem.

cards.q: A columnist writes 2,000 furious words attacking a film, mocking its director, its cast and everyone who enjoyed it. What has she written?
cards.why: A furious, one-sided attack is a diatribe. A eulogy praises, an anthology is a collection and a synopsis is a neutral summary.

words.meaning: Understood by, or meant for, only a small group with special knowledge
words.note: Greek esoterikos = belonging to an inner circle.

cards.q: The comedian's jokes about medieval tax law were too ___ for the crowd; only two historians laughed.
cards.why: Jokes only specialists get are esoteric. Exotic means foreign and striking, eclectic means drawn from varied sources and erratic means unpredictable.

o: The forum hosts esoteric debates about rare coin mintmarks.
Her esoteric outfit came straight from a market in Morocco.
His esoteric playlist mixed jazz, ghazals and heavy metal.
The esoteric train arrived at a different time every day.
cards.why: Esoteric means understood by a small, specialist group. The wrong sentences confuse it with exotic, eclectic and erratic.

words.meaning: Show or declare that someone is not guilty
words.note: Latin ex = out of + culpa = blame, the same culpa as culpable.

cards.q: The CCTV footage helped ___ the security guard, proving he was nowhere near the vault that night.
cards.why: Proving he was elsewhere clears him: exculpate. Inculpate is the opposite (to incriminate), extrapolate means to infer from known data and expatriate means to send out of one's country.

cards.q: Far from implicating her, the leaked emails actually ___ the accountant: they showed she had warned the board twice.
cards.why: 'Far from implicating her' signals the reverse: the emails cleared her. Implicated, incriminated and indicted all point toward guilt.

words.meaning: Overused and therefore dull; unoriginal
words.note: From Hackney in London, once known for horses hired out to anyone; a 'hackney' became a worn-out, overworked horse.

cards.q: Examiners groan at essays that open with the ___ line 'Since time immemorial, man has...'
cards.why: A line every examiner has seen a thousand times is overused: hackneyed. Haphazard means random, harrowing means distressing and hallowed means sacred.

o: The hackneyed plot followed every rom-com cliché in order.
The hackneyed tree had been cut down by the storm last night.
Her hackneyed idea was so original that it won first prize.
His hackneyed breathing showed how hard he had run.
cards.why: Hackneyed means worn out by overuse. The wrong sentences take it to mean hacked, original and laboured.

idioms.meaning: A happy, peaceful time in the past, remembered fondly
idioms.origin: Greek myth said the halcyon (kingfisher) calmed the sea for fourteen days each winter so it could nest on the waves.
idioms.caption: Calm seas you remember long after.

cards.q: My grandfather still talks about the halcyon days of his college life in the 1970s. What does he mean?
o: A calm, happy time he looks back on fondly
A troubled time he has never quite got over
A busy time when he worked hardest of all
A wild time full of risks he now regrets
cards.why: Halcyon days are an idealised, happy past. None of the troubled, hectic or regretful readings fit.

cards.q: Before streaming and smartphones, the family gathered every Sunday to watch one film together. Those were ___.
cards.why: A fondly remembered peaceful time. Bread and circuses is entertainment used to keep people quiet, which isn't what this nostalgia is about.

idioms.meaning: Clear signs that something bad, especially failure, is coming
idioms.origin: From the Book of Daniel: at King Belshazzar's feast a hand wrote on the wall, foretelling the fall of his kingdom that very night.
idioms.caption: The message was there for anyone willing to read it.

cards.q: With sales falling every quarter and three senior managers gone, the staff could see the writing on the wall. Meaning?
o: Clear signs that the firm would soon fail
Official notices about new rules for the staff
Rumours that nobody in the office believed
Hints that a big promotion was on the way
cards.why: Falling sales and departures are warning signs of failure. The idiom isn't about literal notices or rumours.

cards.q: When the landlord doubled the rent and footfall halved, the shop owner saw ___ and began planning a closing-down sale.
o: the thin end of the wedge
cards.why: He read clear signs of coming failure and acted. The sword of Damocles is a threat hanging over someone while things still seem fine; here the decline is already visible.

words.meaning: Casually unconcerned; carefree
words.note: French in- not + soucier = to worry.

cards.q: Minutes before the final exam, he lounged in the corridor with an ___ grin, as though it were just another Tuesday.
cards.why: Treating a final like 'just another Tuesday' is carefree: insouciant. Apprehensive and impatient suggest worry or restlessness, and earnest means serious.

o: She signed the huge cheque with an insouciant flick of the wrist.
The insouciant student revised every chapter in a panic all night.
His insouciant reply was full of worried questions about the plan.
The insouciant milk turned sour after a day out of the fridge.
cards.why: Insouciant means casually unconcerned. The wrong sentences use it for panicky, worried and spoiled.

words.meaning: Fearless; adventurous
words.note: Latin in- not + trepidus = alarmed. Trepidation is its opposite.

cards.q: A 19-year-old sails solo around the world, crossing storm-lashed oceans with no support boat. Which word fits her?
cards.why: Facing storms alone takes fearlessness: intrepid. Insipid means dull, indolent means lazy and indigent means very poor.

o: Intrepid reporters stayed in the city as the shelling worsened.
The intrepid child hid behind the sofa whenever thunder rolled.
The soup was intrepid, with hardly any salt or flavour.
The intrepid student napped through every lecture he attended.
cards.why: Intrepid means fearless. The wrong sentences use it for timid, bland and lazy.

words.meaning: Say harmful, untrue things about someone; slander
words.note: Latin malignus = evil-natured. Malignant shares the root.

cards.q: Rival politicians tried to ___ her as corrupt, though no charge against her was ever proven.
cards.why: Spreading unproven charges is slander: malign. Malinger means to fake illness to avoid work, maintain means to keep up and align means to line up.

cards.q: Fact-checkers found that the viral video had been edited to ___ a respected doctor, not to inform viewers.
cards.why: Edited 'not to inform' points to an intent to damage his reputation: malign. Praise and protect run the other way, and quote is neutral.

words.meaning: Extremely generous, especially with money
words.note: Latin munus = gift + facere = to make.

cards.q: A ___ donor paid for the entire new library wing and asked for no plaque in return.
cards.why: Paying for a whole wing is extreme generosity: munificent. Magnificent means splendid to look at, mundane means ordinary and municipal means run by a city.

o: Thanks to a munificent alumna, every student gets a free laptop.
The munificent miser refused to lend even ten rupees.
The munificent palace glittered with gold domes and marble halls.
The munificent office issued new rules on parking.
cards.why: Munificent means lavishly generous. The others confuse it with stingy, magnificent and municipal.

words.meaning: Noisy and difficult to control
words.note: Latin obstreperus = clamorous (strepere = to make a noise).

cards.q: A class of thirty eight-year-olds shouts, throws paper planes and ignores every attempt to quieten it. Which word describes the class?
cards.why: Noisy and hard to control: obstreperous. Conscientious means diligent, contemplative means thoughtful and apprehensive means anxious.

o: Obstreperous fans kept chanting after the match was halted.
The obstreperous mouse crept silently past the sleeping cat.
Her obstreperous bow showed great respect to the visiting guests.
The obstreperous scholar spoke softly and never raised his voice.
cards.why: Obstreperous means noisy and unruly. The wrong sentences use it to mean silent, deferential and soft-spoken.

idioms.meaning: A burden, often from a past mistake, that you cannot get rid of
idioms.origin: From Coleridge's poem The Rime of the Ancient Mariner (1798): a sailor who shoots an albatross is made to wear the dead bird around his neck.
idioms.caption: The mistake you have to keep carrying.

cards.q: The failed project from 2019 has become an albatross around his neck; it comes up in every review. Meaning?
o: A past mistake that keeps weighing on him
A lucky break that later brought success
A rival who keeps blocking his progress
A secret he has never told anyone at work
cards.why: It is a burden from a past failure that he can't shake off. A rival or a secret doesn't match the idea of a mistake that follows him.

cards.q: The huge loan taken to buy the loss-making mill became ___ for the family business for decades.
o: the thin end of the wedge
a Hobson's choice for its owners
cards.why: A long-lasting burden from a bad decision is an albatross. The writing on the wall would be a warning sign, not the burden itself, and Hobson's choice is a take-it-or-leave-it offer.

idioms.meaning: Stop trying because you are satisfied with past success
idioms.origin: Winners at ancient Greek games were crowned with laurel wreaths; 'resting' on them means relying on old glory.
idioms.caption: Yesterday's trophy, today's sofa.

cards.q: After topping the first mock, Priya rested on her laurels and barely studied for the next month. What did she do?
o: She coasted on her earlier success
She celebrated her win with her whole family
She took a well-earned break to avoid burnout
She worried she couldn't repeat her success
cards.why: Resting on your laurels means coasting on an earlier achievement. A 'well-earned break' sounds positive; the idiom is a criticism.

cards.q: The startup that once disrupted the market has ___; it hasn't launched a new product in five years.
o: cut off its nose to spite its face
cards.why: Coasting on old success with no new products is resting on your laurels. Crossing the Rubicon is a bold, irreversible step, the opposite of standing still.

words.meaning: Very clear, in meaning or in appearance
words.note: Latin per = through + lucidus = clear, bright.

cards.q: Her ___ explanation made a chapter that had confused everyone suddenly easy to follow.
cards.why: An explanation that makes a confusing chapter easy is crystal clear: pellucid. Pedantic means fussing over small details, prolix means long-winded and perfunctory means careless.

o: The pellucid lake water showed every pebble on the bed.
The pellucid report was so muddled that nobody could follow it.
Her pellucid voice was too faint to be heard above the traffic.
The pellucid fog hid the hills completely until noon.
cards.why: Pellucid means crystal clear. The wrong sentences use it for muddled, faint and murky.

words.meaning: A strong liking or habitual tendency
words.note: French pencher = to lean.

cards.q: Known for his ___ for dramatic entrances, the actor arrived at the premiere on horseback.
cards.why: A habitual liking: penchant. A pennant is a flag, a pendulum swings, and penance is punishment taken on for wrongdoing.

cards.q: Whenever she travels, Meera hunts for the oldest bookshop in town, a habit she has had since childhood. What does she have for old bookshops?
cards.why: A long-standing fondness is a penchant. An aversion is a strong dislike, ambivalence is mixed feelings and apathy is lack of interest.

words.meaning: Cause something, usually bad, to happen suddenly or sooner than expected
words.note: Latin praeceps = headlong. As an adjective it means hasty.

cards.q: A single unpaid loan was enough to ___ the collapse of the already fragile bank.
cards.why: Bringing the collapse on suddenly: precipitate. Precede means come before, participate means take part and predicate means base on.

cards.q: The minister's careless remark did not cause the protests on its own, but it did ___ them, turning simmering anger into street marches overnight.
cards.why: Turning simmering anger into marches overnight means it hastened them: precipitate. Prevent and extinguish say the opposite, and investigate is unrelated.

words.meaning: Having a long-established habit that is unlikely to change
words.note: Latin inveterare = to make old (vetus = old, as in veteran).

cards.q: An ___ gambler, he promised to quit after every loss and was back at the table within a week.
cards.why: Promising to quit and returning every time shows a deep-rooted habit: inveterate. Invertebrate means without a backbone, innocuous means harmless and inaudible means unable to be heard.

o: An inveterate traveller, she has seen sixty countries and wants more.
He is an inveterate smoker; he lit his very first cigarette yesterday.
The inveterate snail, like all molluscs, has no backbone.
The beginner, inveterate at chess, played her first game today.
cards.why: Inveterate means long-established and hard to change. The wrong sentences use it for something brand new and confuse it with invertebrate.

words.meaning: Strongly reminiscent of something; or smelling strongly of it
words.note: Latin redolere = to give off a smell.

cards.q: The old railway station, with its brass bells and wooden benches, is ___ of the 1940s.
cards.why: Redolent of means strongly reminding you of. Reluctant means unwilling, resilient means quick to recover, and relevant means connected (and takes 'to', not 'of').

o: The kitchen was redolent of cardamom and freshly fried puris.
She felt redolent about joining, and agreed only after much pleading.
The redolent rubber band snapped back into shape instantly.
His redolent answer had nothing to do with the question.
cards.why: Redolent means smelling of or evoking something. The wrong sentences confuse it with reluctant, resilient and irrelevant.

idioms.meaning: Waste time on trivial things while a serious crisis unfolds
idioms.origin: Roman historians accused Emperor Nero of singing and playing music during the great fire of Rome in AD 64. The 'fiddle' came later; violins didn't exist then.
idioms.caption: Music in the palace, flames in the streets.

cards.q: As the floodwaters rose, the council debated the colour of new street signs. Critics said they were fiddling while Rome burned. Meaning?
o: Fussing over trivia while a crisis grew
Making the crisis worse on purpose for gain
Celebrating too early before a crisis ended
Blaming others for a crisis they had caused
cards.why: Debating sign colours during a flood is fussing over trifles while disaster unfolds. The council isn't worsening the flood or blaming anyone.

cards.q: While the company lost its biggest clients, the board spent three meetings redesigning the logo. They were ___.
cards.why: Trivial work during a serious crisis is fiddling while Rome burns. Resting on their laurels is complacency after success; the stress here is on trivia during disaster.

idioms.meaning: Show deep, public regret for something you have done
idioms.origin: In the Bible, people mourning or repenting wore rough sackcloth and put ashes on their heads.
idioms.caption: Rough cloth, ashes, and a public apology.

cards.q: After the data leak, the company's founder appeared on television in sackcloth and ashes. What does that mean?
o: He publicly showed deep regret for the leak
He was dressed very casually for the interview
He refused to accept any blame for the leak
He announced he was selling the company
cards.why: It is a figurative show of penitence; he didn't literally wear sacks. Refusing blame is the opposite.

cards.q: The minister doesn't need to wear ___ over a small typo; a quick correction will do.
cards.why: Sackcloth and ashes is heavy, public repentance, overkill for a typo. Wearing your heart on your sleeve means openly showing your feelings in general, not making a public apology.

words.meaning: Showing sound judgement and deep wisdom
words.note: Latin sagax = keen-scented, shrewd.

cards.q: The ___ old farmer predicted the drought months before the experts, simply by watching the birds and the wells.
cards.why: Reading the signs before the experts did shows wisdom: sagacious. Salacious means crude or lewd, sanctimonious means smugly self-righteous and spacious means roomy.

o: Her sagacious advice saved the firm from a disastrous takeover.
The sagacious remark made the whole room cringe at its rudeness.
He was too sagacious to understand even the simplest instruction.
The sagacious hall could seat over two thousand guests.
cards.why: Sagacious means wise. The wrong sentences use it for rude, dim-witted and roomy.

words.meaning: False or fake, though made to look genuine; based on faulty reasoning
words.note: Latin spurius = illegitimate. Compare specious: a specious argument sounds right but isn't; a spurious thing is simply false.

cards.q: The lawyer showed that the will was ___: the signature had been forged a decade after the man's death.
cards.why: A forged document is fake: spurious. Specious describes an argument that sounds right but isn't; sporadic means occasional and superfluous means unnecessary.

cards.q: Ice-cream sales and drowning deaths rise together every summer, but any claim that one causes the other is ___; hot weather drives both.
cards.why: The link is false: heat drives both. Conclusive and irrefutable say the opposite, and intuitive means instinctively understood.

words.meaning: Calm and showing little emotion; dependable but unexcitable
words.note: Latin stolidus = dull, slow.

cards.q: While the crowd screamed and wept, the ___ security guard stood motionless, his face showing nothing.
cards.why: Showing nothing amid screaming is unemotional calm: stolid. Squalid means filthy, sordid means morally low, and strident means loud and harsh, the opposite of motionless.

cards.q: Whether his team wins the final or loses by an innings, the veteran coach's expression never changes. Which word describes him?
cards.why: An unchanging expression through triumph and defeat is stolid. Volatile, effusive and hysterical all mean showing emotion freely or wildly.

words.meaning: Unnecessary; more than is needed
words.note: Latin super = over + fluere = to flow: overflowing.

cards.q: Cut every ___ word from your summary; examiners reward precision, not padding.
cards.why: 'Not padding' tells you to remove unneeded words: superfluous. Essential and indispensable are the opposite, and ambiguous means unclear, which is a different fault.

o: With two chargers already, a third one seemed superfluous.
Water is superfluous to life; no creature survives without it.
The wound was superfluous, just a scratch on the skin.
She gave a superfluous performance, the finest of her career.
cards.why: Superfluous means more than needed. The wrong sentences confuse it with essential, superficial and superb.

words.meaning: Experienced through another person's actions rather than your own
words.note: Latin vicarius = substitute; a vicar was originally a stand-in for a bishop.

cards.q: Stuck at home, he took ___ pleasure in his friend's travel photos from Ladakh.
cards.why: Enjoying a trip through someone else's photos is vicarious pleasure. Voracious means hungry or eager, various means several and vivacious means lively.

o: Parents feel a vicarious thrill when their child wins a race.
She ate with vicarious hunger, finishing three plates in minutes.
The vicarious host kept the party lively and laughing all night.
He bought vicarious items: pens, tape, string and glue.
cards.why: Vicarious means felt through someone else. The wrong sentences confuse it with voracious, vivacious and various.

idioms.idiom: Kill the goose that lays the golden eggs
idioms.meaning: Destroy a steady source of profit through greed or short-sightedness
idioms.origin: Aesop's fable: a farmer whose goose lays one golden egg a day cuts it open to get all the gold at once, and finds none.
idioms.caption: One golden egg a day wasn't enough.

cards.q: Doubling the coaching fees overnight might bring quick cash, but the institute risks killing the goose that lays the golden eggs. Meaning?
o: Ruining a steady income through greed
Losing its best teachers to a rival
Spending more money than it earns
Being too cautious to grow its business
cards.why: Greedy fee hikes could drive away the students who are its steady income. It isn't about overspending or staff leaving.

cards.q: The town banned its annual fair to collect a one-time land fee, and lost the tourists who kept its shops alive. Which idiom fits?
o: Cutting off its nose to spite its face
cards.why: Killing the golden goose (the short form) means sacrificing a steady source of profit for a quick gain. Robbing Peter to pay Paul shifts a problem rather than destroying the source, and there's no spite here.

idioms.meaning: An impressive show built to hide an ugly or poor reality
idioms.origin: Legend says Grigory Potemkin put up fake village fronts to impress Empress Catherine II on her 1787 tour of Crimea. Historians doubt it, but the phrase stuck.
idioms.caption: All front, no village.

cards.q: Critics called the new 'smart city' district a Potemkin village: glossy towers on the main road, with no water supply behind them. What are they saying?
o: Its glossy look hides a poor reality
It was built far too quickly to last long
It copies a famous design from abroad
It is too costly for ordinary residents
cards.why: Glossy towers with no water behind them: a showpiece masking failure. The idiom is about deception, not speed or cost.

cards.q: Before the inspectors arrived, the school painted only the front corridor and hid the broken desks in a locked room. It was ___.
cards.why: Staging a good-looking front to hide the real state is a Potemkin village. The emperor's new clothes is about people pretending to admire something that isn't there; here the school itself builds the facade.

words.meaning: Very talkative
words.note: Latin loqui = to speak, the root of eloquent and soliloquy.

o: Our loquacious guide filled every bus ride with stories and never paused.
The loquacious note on the board said only 'Class cancelled today'.
She was too loquacious to speak to anyone all evening.
His loquacious handwriting defeated every examiner who ever tried to read it.
cards.why: Loquacious means talkative. The wrong sentences use it for brief (laconic), shy and illegible.

cards.q: The host was so ___ that the guest barely got a word in.
cards.why: Loquacious is talkative. Lugubrious means mournful, ludicrous means absurd and luminous means glowing.

words.meaning: Short and full of meaning
words.note: From pith, the core inside a stem. A pithy line is all core and no padding.

cards.q: The editor cut the three-page tribute to one ___ paragraph that said more than the original.
cards.why: The cut made it shorter and better, which is pithy. The other three all mean long-winded.

cards.q: A speaker ends a two-hour debate with one short line that settles the question. That line is best described as ___.
cards.why: Short and decisive is pithy. Prolix and discursive mean long-winded; florid means overdecorated.

words.meaning: Mocking in a bitter, scornful way
words.note: Greek sardonios, from a Sardinian plant said to twist the face into a grin.

o: He congratulated the winner with a sardonic smile that fooled nobody.
She gave a sardonic account of the facts, plain and free of opinion.
The sardonic nurse comforted the frightened child until the crying finally stopped.
They sat in sardonic silence, too moved by the music to speak.
cards.why: Sardonic is bitter mockery. The wrong sentences use it for neutral, kind and reverent.

cards.q: His ___ praise of the minister's 'brilliant' three-hour speech drew nervous laughter.
cards.why: The praise is mockery, so sardonic. Sanguine means hopeful, sonorous means deep-sounding and sartorial refers to clothes.

words.meaning: Sharp and incisive, especially in criticism
words.note: French trancher = to cut. A trenchant remark cuts to the bone.

cards.q: Her ___ analysis exposed in two pages what the committee had missed in two years.
cards.why: Two pages that expose what two years missed is sharp and incisive. Tepid is half-hearted, tangential is off the point, tentative is unsure.

o: The review was trenchant, naming the exact flaw every other critic avoided.
He made a trenchant apology and promised never to repeat it.
Her trenchant kindness towards the new students won her friends across the whole hostel.
The trenchant speech wandered for an hour and reached no point.
cards.why: Trenchant describes sharp criticism or analysis, not apologies, kindness or waffle.

words.meaning: Calm and hard to excite
words.note: One of the four medieval humours: phlegm was thought to make a person slow to anger.

o: Phlegmatic even as the results loaded, he opened the page without flinching.
She turned phlegmatic at the news and shouted at everyone who came into the room.
The phlegmatic crowd roared at every single boundary.
He was too phlegmatic to sit still for more than a minute.
cards.why: Phlegmatic is unshakeable calm. The wrong sentences describe rage, excitement and restlessness.

cards.q: A captain whose expression never changes, whether the team is winning or collapsing, is best described as ___.
cards.why: An unchanging expression under pressure is phlegmatic. Mercurial means changeable, petulant means sulky and choleric means quick to anger.

idioms.meaning: To clear away a mess of corruption or neglect that has built up for years
idioms.origin: Hercules' fifth labour. King Augeas kept 3,000 oxen in stables that had not been cleaned for thirty years, so Hercules diverted two rivers through them.
idioms.caption: Thirty years of filth. One diverted river.

cards.q: The new principal spent her first year sacking the contractors, auditing the accounts and rewriting the rules. Staff said she had cleaned the Augean stables. What does that mean?
o: Cleared a long-standing mess of corruption and neglect
Worked harder than anyone else was willing to
Made a great show of reform without changing anything at all
Took on a task that could never be finished
cards.why: The idiom is about clearing filth that has been allowed to pile up for years, which is exactly what the audit and the sackings did.

cards.q: The auditor found twenty years of forged bills, cancelled every contract and started the department again from scratch. She had ___.
cards.why: Clearing years of accumulated rot is the Augean stables. Pandora's box releases new troubles, carrying coals to Newcastle is pointless duplication, crossing the Rubicon is an irreversible step.

idioms.meaning: A great fuss over something trivial
idioms.origin: The image is old; Cicero wrote of raising storms in a ladle. The teacup version settled into British English in the 1800s.
idioms.caption: All that weather, in a cup.

cards.q: Two members argued for an hour about the font on the notice board. The secretary called it a storm in a teacup. He meant it was ___.
o: A great deal of fuss over something trivial
A quarrel that was certain to turn serious
A disagreement nobody dared raise openly
A small problem that signalled a much bigger one
cards.why: The fuss was large and the matter tiny. The last option is the thin end of the wedge, which is a different idea.

cards.q: The papers ran three days of headlines on a cricketer's haircut, then dropped it entirely. The whole affair was ___.
o: the thin end of the wedge
cards.why: Enormous noise over nothing is a storm in a teacup. A red herring is a deliberate distraction, which nobody planted here.

words.meaning: Easily made angry
words.note: Latin ira = anger, the root of irate and ire.

o: Our irascible neighbour complains about the noise before the party begins.
The irascible host made every late guest feel entirely at ease.
She was irascible about the deadline and finished the whole report a full week early.
He grew irascible with joy when the results were announced.
cards.why: Irascible means quick to anger, not welcoming, diligent or joyful.

cards.q: Age had made him ___: a misplaced newspaper was now enough to start a row.
cards.why: A row over a newspaper shows a short temper. Amiable is friendly, indifferent is uncaring, reticent is reserved.

words.meaning: Friendly and easy to talk to
words.note: Latin affari = to speak to. An affable person is one you can easily speak to.

cards.q: The chairman was ___ with the juniors, asking about their families before the meeting began.
cards.why: Asking after families is warm and easy, so affable. The other three are all distant or harsh.

o: An affable guard waved us through and asked how the exam had gone.
The affable officer refused to meet anyone without a written appointment.
She gave an affable glare that silenced the entire classroom.
His affable memory held every date from the last decade.
cards.why: Affable describes warm, easy manner. A glare cannot be affable, and memory has no manner at all.

words.meaning: Behaving as though superior to everyone else
words.note: Latin supercilium = eyebrow. The word pictures one eyebrow raised in disdain.

o: A supercilious glance at my shoes told me what he thought of the invitation.
The supercilious waiter apologised twice and refilled the water glasses himself.
She was supercilious about the plan and backed it with her own money.
He wore a supercilious coat that kept out the worst of the rain.
cards.why: Supercilious is looking down on others. It cannot describe an apology, enthusiasm or a coat.

cards.q: The ___ assistant answered every question as though it were beneath him.
cards.why: Treating questions as beneath him is supercilious. Superficial means shallow, superfluous means unnecessary, supercritical is a term from physics.

words.meaning: Casually unconcerned
words.note: Old French nonchaloir = not to care. The -chal- is the heat in calorie: the nonchalant stay cool.

cards.q: He was ___ about the interview, as though a seat at IIM were a small matter.
cards.why: Treating a big thing as small is nonchalance. Anxious is its opposite; earnest and preoccupied both suggest he was taking it very seriously.

cards.q: A student scrolls her phone while the merit list is read out, and shrugs when her own name comes up. Her manner is best described as ___.
cards.why: The shrug is studied unconcern. Obsequious is fawning, fastidious is fussy about detail, diffident is shy rather than unbothered.

words.meaning: Someone who refuses to follow the group
words.note: Samuel Maverick, a Texas rancher, left his calves unbranded, so any unbranded animal became a maverick.

o: A maverick in a house of lawyers, she took up archaeology instead.
The maverick followed every rule in the handbook to the letter.
He was the maverick of the group, agreeing with whoever spoke last.
Her maverick notes were the neatest in the entire class.
cards.why: A maverick breaks from the herd, so following rules or agreeing with everyone contradicts it.

cards.q: The committee wanted a safe choice and got a ___ who rewrote the syllabus in a month.
cards.why: Rewriting the syllabus against expectation is a maverick's move. A conformist and a functionary do what is expected.

idioms.meaning: A hidden weakness in someone widely admired
idioms.origin: From the Book of Daniel: Nebuchadnezzar dreams of a towering statue with a head of gold and feet of clay, which shatters when the feet are struck.
idioms.caption: Gold at the top. Clay at the bottom.

cards.q: The biography revealed that the reformer had quietly taken money from the firms he attacked in public. Reviewers said he had feet of clay. They meant he had ___.
o: A hidden flaw in a figure everyone admired
A refusal to act when action was needed
A humble background he had tried to conceal
A slow and unsteady way of working
cards.why: The idiom is about a secret weakness in an admired person, not about hesitation, origins or pace.

cards.q: For twenty years she was the conscience of the movement. Then the letters surfaced, and even her admirers admitted she had ___.
cards.why: A revealed flaw in an admired figure is feet of clay. An albatross is a burden of guilt carried openly, not a secret weakness.

idioms.meaning: To take the credit or attention that belonged to another
idioms.origin: John Dennis, an 18th-century playwright, invented a thunder machine for his own play. The play failed, and he then heard his machine being used by a rival company.
idioms.caption: His thunder. Someone else's play.

cards.q: A junior researcher presented the team's findings the day before her supervisor's scheduled talk. He accused her of stealing his thunder, meaning she had ___.
o: Taken the attention that was due to him
Published work that was not hers to publish
Criticised him in front of the department
Used his method without asking permission
cards.why: Stealing thunder is about taking someone's moment, not about theft of the work itself.

cards.q: The minister announced the scheme at a press conference an hour before the chief minister's rally. The papers said he had ___.
o: thrown the baby out with the bathwater
cards.why: Getting in first and taking the moment is stealing thunder. Throwing the baby out with the bathwater would mean discarding something good along with the bad.

words.meaning: Kept secret, usually because it would not be approved
words.note: Latin clam = secretly.

cards.q: Their ___ meetings in the old library ended the day the warden read the register.
cards.why: Being caught out by a register shows the meetings were meant to be secret. Convivial is cheerful, compulsory is required, unremarkable means ordinary.

o: A clandestine group met after midnight to print the banned pamphlet.
The clandestine ceremony was broadcast live to four states.
He made a clandestine announcement in the morning assembly.
Their clandestine friendship was the talk of every corridor in the building.
cards.why: Clandestine means hidden, so broadcasts, assemblies and corridor gossip all contradict it.

words.meaning: Deliberately treacherous
words.note: Latin per fidem decipere = to deceive through trust. It is the opposite of fidelity.

o: A perfidious ally signed our treaty in the morning and the enemy's by night.
The perfidious officer refused the bribe and reported the man who offered it.
She was perfidious in her duties and never once missed a shift.
His perfidious generosity paid the fees of six students.
cards.why: Perfidious is betrayal of trust, so honesty, reliability and generosity all contradict it.

cards.q: The ___ secretary passed every internal plan to the rival firm.
cards.why: Passing plans to a rival is betrayal, so perfidious. Punctilious means careful about detail, pernicious means quietly destructive, prodigious means huge.

words.meaning: Cunning used to deceive
words.note: An old cousin of wile. Someone with none of it is guileless.

cards.q: He had no money, no title and no connections, and won the case by sheer ___.
cards.why: Winning without resources points to cunning. Candour is frankness, gravitas is seriousness, diligence is hard work.

cards.q: A negotiator wins by letting the other side believe they are getting the better deal. His weapon is ___.
cards.why: Engineering a false impression is guile. Probity is honesty, temerity is reckless boldness, zeal is enthusiasm.

words.meaning: Understood without being stated
words.note: Latin tacere = to be silent, the root of taciturn.

cards.q: Nobody approved the arrangement aloud, yet it ran for years with everyone's ___ consent.
cards.why: Consent that was never spoken is tacit. Written and formal are the opposite; grudging describes reluctance, not silence.

o: Her silence at the meeting was taken as tacit approval of the plan.
He gave tacit instructions in a signed circular sent to all departments.
The tacit announcement was read out twice over the public address.
They argued tacitly for an hour and the whole floor could hear it.
cards.why: Tacit means unspoken, so circulars, announcements and audible arguing all contradict it.

words.meaning: Harmless
words.note: Latin in- (not) + nocere (to harm), the same root as noxious.

cards.q: What seemed an ___ question turned out to decide the entire case.
cards.why: The question looked harmless, so innocuous. Incongruous means out of place, inexorable means unstoppable, inveterate means long-established.

o: An innocuous remark about the weather somehow started the quarrel.
The innocuous chemical burned through the steel tray in seconds.
He was given an innocuous warning and suspended for a year.
Her innocuous attack on the proposal left the entire committee in ruins.
cards.why: Innocuous means harmless, so burning, suspension and ruin all contradict it.

idioms.meaning: A show of affection that hides a betrayal
idioms.origin: In the Gospels, Judas identifies Jesus to the soldiers by greeting him with a kiss.
idioms.caption: The greeting was the signal.

cards.q: He praised his colleague warmly at the farewell, having already sent the complaint that cost the man his job. The praise was a Judas kiss, meaning ___.
o: A show of friendship concealing a betrayal
A kindness offered far too late to help
An apology made only because others were watching
A compliment designed to embarrass the person praised
cards.why: A Judas kiss is warmth used as cover for betrayal, which is exactly what the complaint makes it.

cards.q: She embraced her rival on stage, knowing the article naming him would run that night. The embrace was ___.
cards.why: Affection masking betrayal is a Judas kiss. Crocodile tears are false grief, a Parthian shot is a hit delivered while leaving.

idioms.meaning: Someone who keeps what they cannot use, purely to stop others having it
idioms.origin: From Aesop: a dog lies in the manger of hay it cannot eat, and growls at the ox that can.
idioms.caption: Can't eat it. Won't let you.

cards.q: He had not opened the lab in two years, yet blocked every request from other departments to use it. Colleagues called him a dog in the manger, meaning he ___.
o: Denied others what he had no use for himself
Guarded the lab because he feared being replaced
Had taken on far more than he could manage
Defended a position long after it was lost
cards.why: The point of the idiom is withholding something useless to you but valuable to others.

cards.q: The flat stood empty for a decade while he refused every tenant and every buyer. A neighbour called him ___.
cards.why: Keeping an unused thing from others is the dog in the manger. A Cassandra makes unheeded warnings, a curate's egg is partly good and partly bad.

words.meaning: A shortage of something
words.note: Latin paucus = few, the same family as few and pauper.

cards.q: The report was rejected for a ___ of evidence, not for any flaw in its reasoning.
cards.why: Rejected for too little evidence, so paucity. Wealth and breadth would mean there was plenty of it.

cards.q: A library holds four books on a subject that needs four hundred. It suffers from a ___ of material.
cards.why: Four where four hundred are needed is a shortage. The other three all mean too much.

words.meaning: Far more than is needed
words.note: Greek plethore = fullness. It began as a medical word for too much blood.

o: A plethora of coaching apps now competes for the same two study hours.
The plethora of applicants was so small the seat went unfilled.
He answered with a plethora, saying nothing at all for a minute.
She faced a plethora of choices and found there were exactly two of them.
cards.why: A plethora is an overwhelming excess, so an unfilled seat, silence and two options all contradict it.

cards.q: The problem is not a shortage of advice but a ___ of it, every piece contradicting the last.
cards.why: The sentence sets 'not a shortage' against the blank, so it must mean too much. The other three all mean too little.

words.meaning: Recklessly wasteful, especially with money
words.note: Latin profligare = to strike down, to ruin.

o: Profligate spending on three new buildings left nothing for salaries.
He was profligate with his savings and retired at forty with a surplus.
Her profligate accounting saved the department a crore this year.
The profligate committee refused to spend a rupee without three signatures.
cards.why: Profligate means wasteful, so surpluses, savings and tight control all contradict it.

cards.q: A ___ heir ran through a fortune that had taken three generations to build.
cards.why: Running through a fortune is profligate. Prolific means highly productive, proficient means skilled, prodigious means enormous.

words.meaning: Rich and luxurious
words.note: Latin opes = wealth and resources, the root of opulence.

cards.q: After the ___ lobby, the rooms upstairs were a shock: bare walls and one bulb.
cards.why: The lobby must contrast with bare walls, so it was luxurious. The other three all match the bare rooms instead.

o: An opulent hall of chandeliers and marble greeted the delegates.
The opulent room held one chair, one table and nothing whatsoever besides.
He led an opulent life on a clerk's pay and saved half of it.
Their opulent meal of rice and salt was eaten in silence.
cards.why: Opulent means richly luxurious, so bare rooms, thrift and plain food all contradict it.

words.meaning: Severely plain, with no comfort or decoration
words.note: Greek austeros = harsh or dry, first used of a taste that dries the tongue.

o: His austere room held a cot, a lamp and a shelf of books.
The austere banquet ran to nine courses and a live orchestra.
She was austere in her giving, supporting every cause she met.
The austere decorations covered every inch of the hall in gold.
cards.why: Austere means bare and severe, so banquets, open-handedness and gold decoration all contradict it.

cards.q: A monk's cell with no decoration, no heating and a single wooden bed is best described as ___.
cards.why: Bare and severe is austere. Palatial and ornate mean grand or decorated; cluttered means full of things.

idioms.meaning: A costly possession that is more trouble than it is worth
idioms.origin: Kings of Siam are said to have given sacred white elephants to courtiers they disliked: the animal could not be worked or given away, and its upkeep ruined the owner.
idioms.caption: A gift you cannot afford to keep.

cards.q: The stadium cost 400 crore, hosted four matches and now costs 2 crore a year to maintain. The press calls it a white elephant, meaning ___.
o: A possession costing far more to keep than it is worth
A project abandoned before it was finished
A showpiece built only to impress visitors
A scheme that enriched only the contractors who built it
cards.why: The whole point is the ruinous upkeep of something that gives little back. The stadium was finished and is still standing.

cards.q: The inherited mansion cannot be sold, cannot be let, and swallows half his income in repairs. It is ___.
cards.why: A possession whose upkeep ruins you is a white elephant. Manna from heaven would be unexpected help, which this is the opposite of.

idioms.meaning: Unexpected help arriving exactly when it is needed
idioms.origin: In Exodus, the Israelites wandering the desert find manna on the ground each morning as food they did nothing to earn.
idioms.caption: Help nobody arranged.

cards.q: The trust was weeks from closing when an old student left it his entire estate. The secretary called the bequest manna from heaven, meaning it was ___.
o: Unexpected help arriving just when it was needed
A reward earned by years of patient work
A gift that came with heavy conditions attached to it
Relief that proved far too small to matter
cards.why: Manna is unearned and unplanned, which rules out the reward option, and it saved the trust, which rules out the last.

cards.q: The monsoon broke on the very day the last well ran dry. For the village the rain was ___.
cards.why: Unlooked-for rescue at the last moment is manna from heaven. A false dawn would be relief that then failed.

words.meaning: To scold someone severely
words.note: Old English upbregdan, to bring a fault up against someone.

o: The coach upbraided the openers for throwing away two hours of good work.
She upbraided him warmly for the kindness he had shown her mother last winter.
He upbraided the proposal by signing it without reading a word.
They upbraided the winner with garlands and a long applause.
cards.why: Upbraid is harsh scolding, so warmth, signatures and garlands all contradict it.

cards.q: The letter did not ___ him; it simply listed what had gone wrong and asked for a reply.
cards.why: The contrast is between scolding and a plain list of facts, so the blank must mean scold.

words.meaning: To reject or disown completely
words.note: Latin repudium = divorce. To repudiate once meant to cast off a spouse.

cards.q: The party was forced to ___ the remark within hours of its spokesman making it.
cards.why: Damage control means publicly disowning the remark, not repeating it, reintroducing it or issuing it again.

o: He repudiated the agreement his predecessor had signed and began fresh talks.
She repudiated the theory by supplying the last proof it needed.
The board repudiated the plan and then voted unanimously to fund every part of it.
He repudiated her advice and followed every word of it.
cards.why: Repudiate means to reject, so proving, funding and following all contradict it.

words.meaning: Offence or resentment at being slighted
words.note: Latin umbra = shade. To take umbrage is to feel overshadowed.

cards.q: He took ___ at being thanked last, and left before the photographs.
cards.why: Walking out over the order of thanks is wounded pride. Take heart means to be encouraged, take charge means to lead.

cards.q: A senior professor finds his name listed after the juniors on the invitation and refuses to attend. What has he taken? ___
cards.why: Offence at a perceived slight is umbrage. Recourse is a remedy sought, refuge is shelter, counsel is advice.

words.meaning: Sharp and bitter in tone
words.note: Latin acerbus = sour or harsh, the same family as acid and acrid.

cards.q: His ___ review of the novel ended the author's friendship with the magazine.
cards.why: A review that ends a friendship is biting, so acerbic. Acoustic relates to sound, ascetic to self-denial, aesthetic to beauty.

o: An acerbic one-line reply ended the discussion and the friendship with it.
Her acerbic praise left the young writer glowing for a week.
He was acerbic with the children, who all adored his gentle bedtime stories.
The acerbic lullaby sent the whole ward peacefully to sleep.
cards.why: Acerbic is bitter sharpness, so glowing praise, gentleness and lullabies all contradict it.

words.meaning: Meant to teach, often too obviously
words.note: Greek didaskein = to teach.

o: The novel turns didactic in the last chapter, stopping the story to lecture.
His didactic silence taught the class nothing at all.
The didactic film left every question wide open and explained nothing whatsoever.
She wrote a didactic poem with no message of any kind.
cards.why: Didactic means teaching or moralising, so teaching nothing and having no message contradict it.

cards.q: Children's books of that era were relentlessly ___: every story stopped to deliver its lesson.
cards.why: Stories that stop to deliver lessons are didactic. Whimsical is playful, cryptic is obscure, lyrical is songlike.

idioms.meaning: Something that looks threatening but has no real power
idioms.origin: An old Chinese expression, zhilaohu, made famous in English by Mao Zedong in 1946 for enemies who appear fearsome but are hollow.
idioms.caption: All roar, no teeth.

cards.q: The commission can summon anyone but cannot punish anyone. Critics call it a paper tiger, meaning it ___.
o: Looks powerful but can do nothing
Acts only when the press is watching
Was created to delay a real inquiry
Is run by people with no expertise
cards.why: A paper tiger is about appearance without power, not about motives or competence.

cards.q: The new regulator issued three warnings in five years and not a single penalty. The industry treats it as ___.
cards.why: Threat without bite is a paper tiger. A sword of Damocles is a threat that genuinely hangs over you.

idioms.idiom: Beard the lion in its den
idioms.meaning: To confront a powerful person on their own ground
idioms.origin: From an older sense of beard, to seize by the beard and so defy. Walter Scott's Marmion made the phrase popular.
idioms.caption: You go to him. On his floor.

cards.q: Rather than write again, she flew to head office and raised the complaint in the chairman's own boardroom. She had bearded the lion in its den, meaning she ___.
o: Confronted a powerful person on his own ground
Took a risk that was certain to fail
Appealed over the head of her own immediate boss
Started a quarrel she could not win
cards.why: The idiom is about where the confrontation happens: on the powerful person's own territory.

cards.q: The junior lawyer argued the point in the senior judge's own court, to his face. She had ___.
o: bearded the lion in its den
cards.why: Facing power on its own ground is bearding the lion. Tilting at windmills is fighting imaginary enemies, and pouring oil calms a quarrel instead of starting one.

words.meaning: Vague, with no clear shape
words.note: Latin nebula = mist or cloud, the same word as the nebula in the night sky.

cards.q: The plan was ___: three slides of ambition and not one number.
cards.why: Ambition without numbers is vague, so nebulous. The other three all describe a plan with hard detail.

o: His answer stayed nebulous, circling the question without ever landing.
The nebulous instructions gave the exact time, the place and the dress code.
She had a nebulous grasp of the formula and derived it from memory.
The nebulous contract ran to 200 pages of precise clauses.
cards.why: Nebulous means vague, so exact instructions, firm command and precise clauses all contradict it.

words.meaning: Showing deep learning
words.note: Latin erudire = to bring out of rudeness, that is, to polish by teaching.

o: An erudite footnote traced the word through four languages in three lines.
The erudite speaker admitted he had never read the book he was there to review.
Her erudite guesswork rested on nothing she had ever studied.
He gave an erudite shrug and quickly changed the subject.
cards.why: Erudite means deeply learned, so admitted ignorance, guesswork and a shrug all contradict it.

cards.q: The lecture was ___, drawing on sources in five languages.
cards.why: Five languages of sources is deep learning. Eroded means worn away, arid means dry, ardent means passionate.

words.meaning: Someone who attacks cherished beliefs or institutions
words.note: Greek eikon (image) + klastes (breaker). The first were destroyers of religious images in 8th-century Byzantium.

cards.q: An ___ by temperament, she spent her career dismantling the theories her teachers had built.
cards.why: Dismantling received theories is iconoclasm. An apologist defends them, a traditionalist upholds them, a custodian preserves them.

cards.q: A historian argues that the nation's most loved freedom fighter was in fact a poor strategist. In doing so he is acting as an ___.
cards.why: Attacking a revered figure is iconoclasm. An archivist keeps records, an ideologue pushes a doctrine, an apologist defends.

words.meaning: The luck of finding something good without looking for it
words.note: Coined by Horace Walpole in 1754 from the Persian tale The Three Princes of Serendip, who kept making happy discoveries by accident.

o: Penicillin came by serendipity: a spoiled dish nobody meant to leave out.
After ten years of planned trials, the vaccine was pure serendipity.
He found the file by serendipity, exactly where the index had said it would be.
Her serendipity was the result of a careful two-year search.
cards.why: Serendipity is accidental good fortune, so planned trials, an index and a deliberate search all contradict it.

cards.q: The discovery owed nothing to the grant and everything to ___: a wrong turn in the archive.
cards.why: A wrong turn that pays off is serendipity. Diligence, a systematic method and precedent all imply finding it deliberately.

words.meaning: A small trace of something that has otherwise vanished
words.note: Latin vestigium = footprint. A vestige is a footprint left by the past.

cards.q: Not a ___ of the old hostel survives except the gate and its iron bell.
cards.why: What survives of something gone is a vestige. A blueprint is a plan, a replica is a copy, a rumour is talk.

o: A single arch is the last vestige of the fort that once stood here.
The vestige of the building covers four acres and is fully in use.
He kept a vestige of the old library: all forty thousand volumes of it.
Vestiges of the new wing will be completed by next spring.
cards.why: A vestige is a small surviving trace, so four acres, forty thousand volumes and future building all contradict it.

idioms.meaning: A single fatal weakness in someone otherwise strong
idioms.origin: Achilles' mother dipped him in the Styx to make him invulnerable, holding him by the heel. That one dry spot was where the arrow found him.
idioms.caption: Armoured everywhere but one inch.

cards.q: Her quant and DI are near perfect, but parajumbles cost her the percentile every single time. Parajumbles are her Achilles' heel, meaning they are ___.
o: The one weakness that undoes all her strength
The part she has neglected out of dislike
The section she finds hardest to finish in time
A weakness she refuses to admit to anyone
cards.why: An Achilles' heel is the single vulnerable point in something otherwise strong, whatever the reason for it.

cards.q: The bridge was built to survive earthquakes, yet one corroded bolt brought down the entire span. That bolt was ___.
o: the thin end of the wedge
cards.why: One small flaw defeating great strength is an Achilles' heel. The writing on the wall would be a warning of doom, not the cause of it.

idioms.meaning: An early success that is never repeated
idioms.origin: From the flintlock musket: the powder in the priming pan sometimes flared brightly without firing the shot.
idioms.caption: A bright flash. No shot.

cards.q: The band's first song was everywhere; the next three sold nothing and they split up. Critics called them a flash in the pan, meaning they were ___.
o: A sudden success that was never repeated
A success built entirely on publicity
A talent ruined by far too much early praise
A short career ended by sheer bad luck
cards.why: A flash in the pan is about the success not lasting. It says nothing about why.

cards.q: He topped one mock, then slid back to his old percentile for the next ten. His teacher feared the score was ___.
cards.why: A single unrepeated success is a flash in the pan. A feather in his cap would be a lasting credit, not a one-off.

words.meaning: Holding on firmly and refusing to give up
words.note: Latin tenere = to hold, as in tenant and retain.

cards.q: Four rejections in, she was ___ enough to send the fifth application the same week.
cards.why: Sending a fifth after four rejections is persistence. Despondent means dejected, casual means indifferent, erratic means unpredictable.

o: A tenacious reporter kept filing the request until the file was released.
The tenacious student dropped the subject after one difficult week of classes.
He was tenacious about the goal and forgot it within a month.
Her tenacious grip slipped the moment anyone argued with her.
cards.why: Tenacious means refusing to let go, so dropping out, forgetting and giving way all contradict it.

words.meaning: Easily frightened and nervous
words.note: Latin timor = fear, the root of timid.

o: A timorous knock at the door was all we heard for a full minute.
The timorous captain charged the enemy line entirely alone.
She gave a timorous roar that silenced the whole hall.
He was timorous enough to demand a refund from the manager twice.
cards.why: Timorous means fearful, so charging alone, roaring and demanding refunds all contradict it.

cards.q: The ___ candidate spoke so softly that the panel twice asked him to repeat himself.
cards.why: Speaking too softly out of nerves is timorous. Tempestuous means stormy, temperate means moderate, timeless means ageless.

words.meaning: Boldly daring, sometimes to the point of cheek
words.note: Latin audere = to dare, which also gives us audacity.

cards.q: It was an ___ plan: eleven men, one van, and the whole afternoon's takings.
cards.why: Eleven men taking an afternoon's takings is daring. Cautious, conventional and orthodox all describe the opposite.

cards.q: A first-time director remakes the most loved film in the language and changes its ending. The attempt is best described as ___.
cards.why: Taking on a classic and changing it is bold. Derivative means unoriginal, perfunctory means done without care, tentative means hesitant.

words.meaning: Idealistic to the point of being impractical
words.note: From Don Quixote, Cervantes' knight who charged at windmills believing them to be giants.

o: His quixotic plan to clean every river in the state began with one bucket.
The quixotic accountant checked every figure twice before signing.
She took a quixotic view and backed only the safest of the four available options.
The quixotic schedule allowed extra time for every likely delay.
cards.why: Quixotic is noble but impractical idealism, so caution, safety and careful planning all contradict it.

cards.q: The campaign was ___ from the start, yet it changed how the city talked about its lakes.
cards.why: The 'yet' sets hopeless idealism against a real effect. Cynical and mercenary describe self-interest, methodical describes good organisation.

words.meaning: The highest point
words.note: From Arabic samt, the path, in samt ar-ras, the path over the head. Its opposite is nadir.

cards.q: She reached the ___ of her career at thirty-one and spent the next decade teaching.
cards.why: The high point of a career is its zenith. Nadir is the lowest point, outset is the beginning, fringe is the edge.

o: At the zenith of its power the empire ran from the Danube to the Euphrates.
The company hit its zenith in the very year it finally filed for bankruptcy.
He was at the zenith of his form, averaging eleven runs a season.
The zenith of the hill was the lowest point on the entire route.
cards.why: A zenith is the highest point, so bankruptcy, eleven runs and the lowest point all contradict it.

idioms.idiom: The straw that broke the camel's back
idioms.meaning: The last small addition that makes a situation collapse
idioms.origin: An English proverb from the 1600s: a camel can carry an enormous load, but one more straw is one too many.
idioms.caption: One straw. That was all it took.

cards.q: He had put up with the delays for a year, but the cancelled leave was the straw that broke the camel's back and he resigned. That phrase means it was ___.
o: The last small thing that made everything collapse
The worst of the many problems he had faced
The one grievance he could actually prove
A trivial matter blown completely out of all proportion
cards.why: The straw is small in itself; what matters is that it came last, on top of everything else. The final option describes a storm in a teacup instead.

cards.q: Ten years of rent rises he absorbed without a word. The new parking charge finally made him move out. That charge was ___.
o: the straw that broke the camel's back
the thin end of the wedge
cards.why: A small last addition that triggers collapse is the straw. The thin end of the wedge would be the first small step, not the last.

idioms.idiom: Put the cart before the horse
idioms.meaning: To do things in the wrong order
idioms.origin: The image goes back at least to Roman writing and has meant reversed logic in English since the 1500s.
idioms.caption: Right parts. Wrong order.

cards.q: They designed the brochure before deciding what the course would actually teach. The director said they had put the cart before the horse, meaning they had ___.
o: Done things in the wrong order
Spent money they did not yet have
Copied a rival's approach too closely
Planned far more than they could deliver
cards.why: The idiom is purely about sequence: the thing that should come second was done first.

cards.q: He booked the hall and printed the tickets before the artist had agreed to come at all. He had ___.
o: put the cart before the horse
cards.why: Doing the later step first is putting the cart before the horse. Gilding the lily is overdecorating something already fine.
